title: Home Depot vs. Walmart: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Home Depot vs. Walmart: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Erin Kennedy, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 15, 2026 at 8:54 AM EST 6 min read
HD
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Deciding whether to invest in Home Depot (NYSE:HD) or Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) involves weighing specialized home improvement expertise against the sheer scale of the world's largest general merchandise retailer.

Home Depot focuses on the specialized market for building materials and professional services, while Walmart relies on its massive grocery business and value-based global reach. Both companies are foundational to the consumer economy, yet they respond differently to shifting interest rates and household budgets.

The case for Home Depot

Home Depot is the world's largest home improvement specialty retailer, catering to both DIY enthusiasts and professional contractors, known as "Pros." The company has intensified its focus on these Pro customers through its Pro Xtra loyalty program and Pro Trade Credit offerings. It recently expanded its capabilities in this segment through the strategic acquisitions of SRS and GMS, which provide distribution for roofing and interior construction products. These moves strengthen its position among retail stocks that serve the residential construction and remodeling markets.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached nearly $169.2 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 2.5% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $14.2 billion. This financial performance reflects steady demand for home renovation projects, even as high interest rates affected the broader housing market at times.

As of its February 2026 balance sheet, Home Depot carries a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 5.1. This value indicates that the company's total liabilities exceed five times its total shareholders' equity. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term obligations with assets that can be converted to cash quickly, is approximately 1.1. In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, free cash flow was close to $12.6 billion.

The case for Walmart

Walmart serves approximately 280 million customers weekly through a vast network of discount stores, warehouse clubs, and e-commerce websites. The company leverages its massive scale to provide low prices on groceries, health and wellness products, and general merchandise across its Walmart U.S. and Sam's Club segments. Its tech-powered omnichannel strategy allows it to compete effectively in the digital marketplace by offering pickup and delivery services that complement its physical footprint in 19 countries.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached roughly $735.8 billion, a 6.2% increase over the preceding 12-month period. Net income was approximately $22.1 billion. This growth demonstrates the resilience of the grocery segment, which continues to drive frequent store visits and online orders even when consumers pull back on discretionary spending.

As of January 2026, Walmart maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.7. This suggests that total liabilities are roughly 70% of shareholder equity, indicating a lower reliance on debt relative to its equity base compared to many industry peers. The current ratio is approximately 0.8, which means short-term liabilities slightly exceed short-term assets. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $14.9 billion.

Risk profile comparison

Home Depot faces risks from intense competition in a fragmented home improvement market and the complex integration of its recent large-scale acquisitions. The company also navigates cybersecurity vulnerabilities and potential data breaches as it increases its reliance on digital platforms and automation. Additionally, Home Depot manages ongoing litigation risks, including a class action lawsuit regarding the alleged unauthorized use of AI-powered license plate readers in its store parking lots.

Walmart must successfully execute its omnichannel strategy and realize benefits from heavy investments in technology and supply chain automation to stay ahead of digital rivals. The company faces significant regulatory and legal risks, including recent settlements related to labor practices and the sale of expired products. Furthermore, Walmart's international operations are exposed to risks from fluctuating currency exchange rates and changes in global trade policies or tariffs.

Valuation comparison

Walmart appears cheaper based on its lower sales multiple, while Home Depot offers a lower entry point relative to its future earnings estimates.

Which stock would I buy for 2027?

Retailers are generally not super attractive stocks to me. For one, their net margins tend to be on the low side. Home Depot's net margin for the 12 months ended in August was 8.4%. Walmart's net margin for roughly the same period was only 3%. However, I do like stocks that reward shareholders with dividends. The home renovation specialist is currently paying a dividend of about 2.7%. Walmart's payout is much more modest, with a yield around 0.8%.

Let's consider the two retail stocks' long-term performance:

WMT data by YCharts

Home Depot has absolutely crushed it. But the tables turn on a shorter time frame:

Walmart has outperformed Home Depot over the past 10 years. Of course, past performance is no guarantee of future results. It would be nice if you'd bought Home Depot decades ago, or Walmart 10 years ago. But for 2027 and beyond, I think Home Depot looks like a better stock. Shares haven't been as strong as those of Walmart recently, but the DIY giant has outperformed the S&P 500. I also like its higher net margin. And you'll be paid a respectable dividend while you wait for growth to reaccelerate.

As consumer habits shift toward value and health, established giants Kraft Heinz (NYSE:KHC) and PepsiCo (NASDAQ:PEP) are competing for both kitchen pantry dominance and a spot in your long-term portfolio.

Kraft Heinz focuses primarily on meal essentials and condiments, while PepsiCo balances a diverse empire of beverages and snacks. Investors often compare them to determine which company offers a better mix of defensive stability and valuation.

The case for Kraft Heinz

Kraft Heinz operates a diverse portfolio of brands among consumer staples stocks, focusing on condiments, cheese, and prepared meals. Its products reach consumers through retail and foodservice channels in approximately 40 countries. Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) accounted for roughly 21% of net sales in 2025, and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached nearly $24.8 billion. This represented a decrease of approximately 1.5% compared to the prior period, continuing a recent downward trend in total sales. The company reported a net loss of close to $3.5 billion, resulting in a negative net margin of roughly 14%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.5. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to measure financial leverage. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, is roughly 1.2. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $3.7 billion.

The case for PepsiCo

PepsiCo manages a vast portfolio of snacks and drinks across 200 countries and territories. Its largest customer is Walmart and its affiliates, which represented nearly 14% of consolidated net revenue in 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though the company maintains a strong global distribution network.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 5, 2026, revenue reached nearly $98.2 billion. This reflects revenue growth of approximately 6.4% over the preceding 12 months, following a period of steady annual increases. The company reported net income of roughly $10.9 billion, resulting in a net margin of approximately 11.1%.

As of Pepsi's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 2.4. The current ratio is approximately 0.9, suggesting short-term liabilities slightly exceed short-term assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $7.7 billion.

Risk profile comparison

Kraft Heinz faces intense competition from both national brands and private label alternatives. Fluctuations in commodity prices and energy costs often impact its bottom line despite active hedging strategies. The company also navigates regulatory risks, including litigation over its "ultra-processed" labels, and uncertainty following the pause of its proposed spin-off in early 2026.

title: Marvell’s 3 new directors hint at its biggest Lumentum risk
detail:
Marvell’s 3 new directors hint at its biggest Lumentum risk
Opeyemi Babalola
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 3:37 PM EST 5 min read

LITE
IGG.L
LRCX
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Marvell Technology (MRVL) agreed this month to buy laser maker Lumentum Holdings (LITE) in a $115 billion all-stock deal. Most of the debate since has been about price. IG Group's Axel Rudolph told Reuters that investors are right to question whether Marvell is overpaying.

A restaurant with a line around the block does not need more customers. It needs a bigger kitchen and cooks who stay. Whoever buys that restaurant inherits both problems from day one.

Marvell's latest move suggests it knows what kind of restaurant it bought. On Thursday, November 12, 2026, the company added three independent directors and expanded its board from seven to ten seats, according to its SEC filing.

Also read: Marvell gives up a third of itself to buy its laser supplier

Marvell picked the finance chief of Lam Research (LRCX), the top people executive at Walmart (WMT) and the CEO of Intuit (INTU).

None of them built a career in optics. That lineup points to Marvell's biggest Lumentum risk, and it is neither price nor technology. It is running a sold-out factory business and keeping the people who run it.

Marvell is buying a waiting list

Lumentum does not have a demand problem. CEO Michael Hurlston told Bloomberg on Friday, October 9, 2026, that the company cannot meet about 70% of demand for some products through 2027. He added that customers are already locking in orders for 2030.

That changes what Marvell is buying. A sold-out supplier does not bring spare output. It brings a queue of customers and the costly job of building enough capacity to serve them.

The calendar makes it worse. Hurlston told Bloomberg that Lumentum will miss about 30% of demand for some other products through 2028.

The deal is expected to close in the first half of that year, according to Reuters. Marvell inherits the shortage before it can fix it.

Enter Doug Bettinger. He has been CFO of Lam Research, which makes chipmaking equipment, since 2013, according to the filing. The filing shows he previously ran finance at Avago Technologies, now Broadcom (AVGO), and spent 11 years in Intel (INTC) finance roles before that.

Factories run on heavy upfront spending and slow payback, a different rhythm from designing chips. Marvell put him on its audit committee as a designated financial expert. That committee oversees how factory spending lands on the books.

Marvell grew its board from seven to ten directors on November 12, 2026, adding executives from Lam Research, Walmart and Intuit ahead of the Lumentum deal.CFOTO / Getty Images
The quieter risk is people

The other two picks went to the compensation committee, per the filing. It shows Donna Morris has led people strategy at Walmart since 2020, after working at Adobe (ADBE) from 2002 and rising to chief human resources officer. It also shows Sasan Goodarzi has been CEO of Intuit since January 2019.

title: Walmart just took another step to beat Costco that could backfire

Walmart just took another step to beat Costco that could backfire
Maurie Backman

WMT
COST
ZIPL.PVT

Trading disclosure

Walmart and Costco are natural competitors. Both retailers have built their businesses around offering shoppers competitive prices, a wide selection of merchandise, and opportunities to save money.

But while the two companies share many similarities, they have different ideas about what keeps customers coming back.

Walmart has increasingly focused on making shopping more convenient, particularly through its growing delivery business. 

Costco, meanwhile, continues to emphasize its in-store experience, giving members reasons to visit and discover products they might not have planned to purchase.

Now, Walmart is making another major investment in convenience that could give it an advantage over its warehouse rival.

Walmart sees delivery as a competitive advantage

On Nov. 5, Walmart announced a new multi-year agreement with drone delivery company Zipline to add 300 drone delivery locations across the United States, expanding a program that has already completed more than 2 million deliveries.

The move gives Walmart another way to attract shoppers who want everyday essentials delivered quickly without making a trip to a store. And that could become an increasingly important competitive advantage as consumers prioritize convenience alongside affordability.

Read more: Costco and Walmart offer very different Thanksgiving meal costs

Walmart's expanded partnership with Zipline will make drone delivery available to more customers nationwide, with tens of thousands of eligible items available for delivery in as fast as 30 minutes in areas where the service operates.

Customers can select drone delivery through Walmart's website or app if their addresses fall within an eligible delivery area. 

Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton highlighted how consumer behavior has changed since the partnership began.

"Five years ago, Walmart and Zipline made our first deliveries together," said Cliffton. "Today, customers order from us multiple times a day. When you can get what you need in 10-30 minutes it takes a huge amount of anxiety out of life. People can plan their lives around their loved ones, not errands."

Walmart also offers several other delivery options, including delivery in 30 minutes or less in select markets and one-hour express delivery.

Expanding those options gives shoppers more reasons to use Walmart for everyday purchases rather than turning to competitors or third-party delivery services. It also creates opportunities for Walmart to increase shopping frequency and build customer loyalty.

title: Warren Buffett Said This 1 Mistake Cost Berkshire About $10 Billion. Here’s How Investors Can Avoid It.
detail:
Warren Buffett Said This 1 Mistake Cost Berkshire About $10 Billion. Here’s How Investors Can Avoid It.
Matt DiLallo, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 10:25 AM EST 5 min read
BRK-B
WMT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Warren Buffett never hid from his investment mistakes. Instead, he wanted to learn from them. One of his most expensive blunders wasn't a bad purchase, but one he never completed.

At Berkshire Hathaway's (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) 2004 annual meeting, Buffett confessed that his worst mistake was Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT). While he initially wanted to buy 100 million shares of the retail giant, Berkshire bought only a small amount because, as the price went up, Buffett waited for it to come back down, which never happened. His reluctance to pay a little more turned out to be a $10 billion mistake.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The mistake wasn't buying a bad stock. It was getting too anchored to a price on a good one. That's a trap almost every investor falls into, and it's easy to avoid once you know what to look for.

Image source: Getty Images.

What actually went wrong

Walmart was exactly the kind of business Buffett wanted to own. It was a dominant low-cost leader. He set his sights on buying 100 million shares at a pre-split price of $23. Buffett bought some shares, but then the price rose slightly. He thought it might come back down, so he waited. That pullback never came. In hindsight, he said paying a little more would have been inconsequential compared to the gains the stock would go on to deliver.

Buffett did try to fix this mistake. Berkshire built a new Walmart stake starting in 2005, which was worth nearly $6 billion by 2016, the year it sold most of it.

The math of waiting

Berkshire's missed gains on Walmart show why anchoring can be so costly. If you think a $50 stock has the potential to gain 50% over the next few years, paying 5% more ($52.50) than your desired price would yield a 43% return. That's not a bad return. Waiting for the price to come back down to your target, on the other hand, risks the entire upside if it never does. A small premium costs you a little in the long run, while a missed position costs you the whole gain.

3 ways to avoid the same mistake

Decide what it's worth before you look at the price. Calculate the estimated future value for a stock you'd be happy to own before you start buying. The target price then becomes a comparison point rather than an anchor.

Set your purchases in advance. Consider splitting the position into thirds: buy one third now, another on a pullback, and the final third on a date you pick regardless of price. That way you won't freeze in the face of a rising price like Buffett.

Compare the extra cost to the upside you expect. Before you pass on a stock because it has risen, run the math. If you expected it to gain 50% from your target price and it now costs 5% more than when you first looked, you would still earn about 43% on this purchase. If that's not a worthwhile return, you might not have as much conviction in the stock as you think.

The risk on the other side

The lesson here isn't to pay any price for a stock. Buffett's Walmart mistake served as a valuable lesson because Walmart's an exceptional business, so paying a few percentage-point premium was small relative to its upside. However, chasing a stock that has already run up, or paying a premium for an average business, are different mistakes. It's fine to pay a little bit more than you'd like for a high-quality business, but don't go overboard.

Don't let your discipline cost you

Patience and price discipline are good habits, but Buffett's Walmart miss shows how they can backfire when a small price gap keeps you out of a great business. Decide what a stock is worth before you buy, set your purchases in advance, and weigh any premium against the upside you expect. That way, your discipline protects you from overpaying without costing you the opportunity.

For the full year, the Zacks Consensus Estimates project earnings of $2.88 per share and a revenue of $751.49 billion, demonstrating changes of +9.09% and +5.37%, respectively, from the preceding year.

Additionally, investors should keep an eye on any recent revisions to analyst forecasts for Walmart. Such recent modifications usually signify the changing landscape of near-term business trends. Therefore, positive revisions in estimates convey analysts' confidence in the business performance and profit potential.

Our research reveals that these estimate alterations are directly linked with the stock price performance in the near future. To utilize this, we have created the Zacks Rank, a proprietary model that integrates these estimate changes and provides a functional rating system.

The Zacks Rank system, which varies between #1 (Strong Buy) and #5 (Strong Sell), carries an impressive track record of exceeding expectations, confirmed by external audits, with stocks at #1 delivering an average annual return of +25% since 1988. The Zacks Consensus EPS estimate has moved 0.05% higher within the past month. Walmart is currently sporting a Zacks Rank of #3 (Hold).

Valuation is also important, so investors should note that Walmart has a Forward P/E ratio of 43.89 right now. This valuation marks a premium compared to its industry average Forward P/E of 13.98.

It's also important to note that WMT currently trades at a PEG ratio of 4.57. The PEG ratio is akin to the commonly utilized P/E ratio, but this measure also incorporates the company's anticipated earnings growth rate. The average PEG ratio for the Retail - Supermarkets industry stood at 2.14 at the close of the market yesterday.
